etymology: From the proper name Nimrod, the "mighty hunter before the LORD" (Gen 10:9). The Oxford English Dictionary’s earliest evidence for the noun is from around 1548, in the writing of John Bale. The American Heritage Dictionary gives two senses, a hunter and, informally, a foolish person. It says the second probably comes from the cartoon character Bugs Bunny mocking the hunter Elmer Fudd as "poor little Nimrod."
biblical_def: In English a nimrod is a hunter, a man given to the chase. The word is the name of the son of Cush: "he began to be a mighty one in the earth. He was a mighty hunter before the LORD" (Gen 10:8–9). Scripture remembers him for more than hunting: "the beginning of his kingdom was Babel" (Gen 10:10). The mighty hunter became the first empire-builder, and his kingdom began at the place where men later tried to make a name for themselves against God. In informal English the word has also come to mean a fool, a sense the American Heritage Dictionary traces, probably, to a cartoon. The Christian observation: Nimrod’s name stands for strength, skill and ambition. Scripture’s question is always what a mighty man builds, and for whose name.
webster_summary: A hunter (OED, from c. 1548); informally a fool. From Nimrod, "a mighty hunter before the LORD," whose kingdom began at Babel (Gen 10:9–10).
webster_full: NIMROD, n. (from c. 1548, OED) A hunter; one devoted to the chase. Informal: a silly or foolish person (American Heritage Dictionary). After Nimrod, son of Cush (Gen 10:8–10).
See also the entry for the man himself, Nimrod.
scriptures: Gen 10:8
And Cush begat Nimrod: he began to be a mighty one in the earth.
Gen 10:9
He was a mighty hunter before the LORD: wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD.
And the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.
corruption_summary: The name of the first mighty man of the earth has slid from "hunter" to "fool." Scripture’s concern is what he built with his might.
corruption_paragraphs: The slang sense is an accident of a cartoon, and the American Heritage Dictionary hedges even that. The older English sense keeps the Bible’s picture of a strong, skilled man of the field.

Genesis does not stop at his skill. The mighty hunter founded a kingdom, and its first city was Babel (Gen 10:10). Strength and ambition are gifts, but they serve either God’s name or man’s. That is the question Nimrod’s story puts to every strong man.
roots_summary: Proper name Nimrod (Gen 10:8–10) → English nimrod, a hunter (OED, c. 1548) → informal sense, a fool (AHD).
roots_lines: Gen 10:9: "a mighty hunter before the LORD"
c. 1548: OED’s earliest evidence for the noun, John Bale
Informal sense: a foolish person (American Heritage Dictionary)
usage: "Every nimrod in the county was in the woods on opening day."
He was a mighty hunter before the LORD. (Gen 10:9).
The beginning of his kingdom was Babel. (Gen 10:10).

pos: noun (a giant; a person or thing of colossal power)
etymology: From the proper name Goliath, the Philistine champion of Gath (1Sa 17:4). The Oxford English Dictionary’s earliest evidence for the noun is from 1607, in the writing of Samuel Hieron, a Church of England clergyman. The American Heritage Dictionary defines it as a person or thing of colossal power or achievement.
biblical_def: A goliath is a giant, a person or thing of overwhelming size or power: a goliath of industry. The word is the name of the champion David faced: "there went out a champion out of the camp of the Philistines, named Goliath, of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span" (1Sa 17:4). English remembers the giant, but Scripture remembers the God who brought him down. David told him, "Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts" (1Sa 17:45), and he gave the reason: "the battle is the LORD’S" (1Sa 17:47). The Christian observation: the story is not mainly about an underdog. It is about God, who "hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty" (1Co 1:27).
webster_summary: A giant; a person or thing of colossal power (OED, from 1607). From Goliath of Gath, felled by David because "the battle is the LORD’S" (1Sa 17:47).
webster_full: GOLIATH, n. (from 1607, OED) A giant; a person or thing of colossal power or achievement (American Heritage Dictionary). After Goliath of Gath (1Sa 17).
See also the entry for the man himself, Goliath.
scriptures: And there went out a champion out of the camp of the Philistines, named Goliath, of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span.

Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied.
And all this assembly shall know that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the LORD'S, and he will give you into our hands.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
corruption_summary: "David and Goliath" now means any upset by an underdog. In Scripture the victory belongs to the LORD of hosts, not to the smaller man’s pluck.
corruption_paragraphs: Sports writers and business pages use the story for any small side that beats a big one, and the hero is the plucky underdog. That leaves God out of a story told to show him. David said the whole assembly would know "that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear" (1Sa 17:47).
The lesson is not that the small always win. It is that God chooses the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty (1Co 1:27).
roots_summary: Proper name Goliath (1Sa 17:4) → English goliath, a giant or colossus (OED, 1607).
roots_lines: 1Sa 17:4: Goliath of Gath, champion of the Philistines
1607: OED’s earliest evidence for the noun, Samuel Hieron
Modern sense: a person or thing of colossal power (AHD)
usage: "The small shop held its own against the retail goliath across the road."
I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts. (1Sa 17:45).
The battle is the LORD’S. (1Sa 17:47).

etymology: From the proper name Methuselah, whose days were "nine hundred sixty and nine years" (Gen 5:27). The Oxford English Dictionary’s earliest evidence for the noun is from 1509, in a translation by H. Watson. The American Heritage Dictionary defines it as an extremely old or long-lived man.
biblical_def: A Methuselah is a very old man, and "as old as Methuselah" means as old as anyone can be. The name belongs to the longest life Scripture records: "And all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty and nine years: and he died" (Gen 5:27). The record ends the way every line of Genesis 5 ends, except Enoch’s: and he died. Moses later set the ordinary span: "The days of our years are threescore years and ten" (Psa 90:10). The Christian observation: the longest life in the Bible still ended. A long life is a gift, but wisdom is knowing it is short: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom" (Psa 90:12).
webster_summary: A very old man (OED, from 1509). After Methuselah, 969 years (Gen 5:27); even the longest life ends, so "teach us to number our days" (Psa 90:12).
webster_full: METHUSELAH, n. (from 1509, OED) An extremely old or long-lived man (American Heritage Dictionary); "as old as Methuselah." After Methuselah, son of Enoch (Gen 5:21–27).
See also the entry for the man himself, Methuselah.
scriptures: Gen 5:27
And all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty and nine years: and he died.
The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away.
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
corruption_summary: "Methuselah" has become a joke about age. Scripture records his years to teach that even the longest life ends in death and judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: We laugh at old age with his name and spend fortunes trying to stretch our own years. Genesis 5 answers with a refrain: "and he died." Nine hundred sixty-nine years did not exempt Methuselah.
The Bible’s counsel is not to fear age but to number our days (Psa 90:12). A man who knows his years are short spends them on what lasts.
roots_summary: Proper name Methuselah (Gen 5:27) → English Methuselah, a very old man (OED, 1509).
roots_lines: Gen 5:27: 969 years, "and he died"
1509: OED’s earliest evidence for the noun, a translation by H. Watson
Idiom: "as old as Methuselah"
usage: "Grandpa called himself the Methuselah of the men’s class."
All the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty and nine years: and he died. (Gen 5:27).
So teach us to number our days. (Psa 90:12).

pos: noun (something enormous in size or power)
etymology: A borrowing from Hebrew bĕhēmōṯ (Oxford English Dictionary), which the American Heritage Dictionary gives as the plural of bĕhēmâ, beast. The OED’s earliest evidence for the word is from before 1382, in the Wycliffite Bible. The American Heritage Dictionary gives the general sense first: something enormous in size or power.
biblical_def: In everyday English a behemoth is anything huge and powerful: a behemoth of a truck, a corporate behemoth. The word is the name of the great beast God showed Job: "Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee; he eateth grass as an ox" (Job 40:15). God speaks of its strength at length, and then says of it, "He is the chief of the ways of God: he that made him can make his sword to approach unto him" (Job 40:19). The Christian observation: in Job, behemoth is not a symbol of power that rivals God. It is a creature God made, "which I made with thee," and the Maker can master it. Whatever behemoth a man faces, God made it and rules it.
webster_summary: Something enormous in size or power. From Hebrew bĕhēmōṯ (in English before 1382, OED), the great beast God made and masters (Job 40:15, 19).
webster_full: BEHEMOTH, n. Something enormous in size or power (American Heritage Dictionary); in Scripture, the great beast of Job 40. From Hebrew, in English from before 1382 (OED).
See also the entry for the creature of Job 40, Behemoth.
scriptures: Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee; he eateth grass as an ox.
He is the chief of the ways of God: he that made him can make his sword to approach unto him.
corruption_summary: Modern use makes a behemoth any giant thing to be feared or admired. In Job it is a creature, made by God and mastered by its Maker.
corruption_paragraphs: Men call a great corporation, a government or a machine a behemoth, and they mean it is beyond anyone’s control. Job learned the opposite. God pointed to the greatest beast he knew and said, "which I made with thee" (Job 40:15).
The point of God’s speech was humility. Job could not tame behemoth, but its Maker could (Job 40:19). No created power, however large, stands outside his rule.
roots_summary: Hebrew bĕhēmōṯ (Job 40:15) → English behemoth (OED, before 1382) → general sense, something enormous.
roots_lines: Job 40:15: "Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee"
Before 1382: OED’s earliest evidence, the Wycliffite Bible
General sense: something enormous in size or power (AHD)
usage: "The new distribution center is a behemoth."
Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee. (Job 40:15).
He that made him can make his sword to approach unto him. (Job 40:19).

etymology: From the proper name Jezebel, the wife of Ahab (1Ki 21:25). The Oxford English Dictionary’s earliest evidence for the noun is from 1558, in the writing of John Knox. The American Heritage Dictionary defines it as a woman regarded as evil and scheming.
biblical_def: To call a woman a Jezebel is to call her wicked and scheming, a woman who uses her power or charm to lead men into sin. The name belongs to the Phoenician queen of Israel. Scripture’s verdict is plain: "there was none like unto Ahab, which did sell himself to work wickedness in the sight of the LORD, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up" (1Ki 21:25). She brought Baal worship into Israel and hunted the prophets of the LORD. The name appears again in Christ’s letter to Thyatira, where "that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess," taught his servants "to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed unto idols" (Rev 2:20). The Christian observation: Scripture uses the name for false religion that seduces God’s people, and it also records mercy offered: "I gave her space to repent" (Rev 2:21).
webster_summary: A wicked, scheming woman (OED, from 1558). After Ahab’s queen, who "stirred up" her husband to wickedness (1Ki 21:25), and the false prophetess of Thyatira (Rev 2:20).
webster_full: JEZEBEL, n. (from 1558, OED) A woman regarded as evil and scheming (American Heritage Dictionary). After Jezebel, wife of Ahab (1Ki 16–21; 2Ki 9).
See also the entry for the queen herself, Jezebel.
scriptures: But there was none like unto Ahab, which did sell himself to work wickedness in the sight of the LORD, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up.
Rev 2:20

Notwithstanding I have a few things against thee, because thou sufferest that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed unto idols.
Rev 2:21
And I gave her space to repent of her fornication; and she repented not.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
corruption_summary: The name is now used loosely as an insult for any woman a man dislikes. Scripture uses it for false religion and seduction into idolatry, and it pairs the warning with a call to repent.
corruption_paragraphs: Men throw "Jezebel" at women who cross them, and it becomes a cheap slur. Scripture is more exact. Jezebel’s sin was idolatry pressed on God’s people and a husband stirred up to evil (1Ki 21:25), and in Thyatira it was false teaching that led Christ’s servants into fornication and idolatry (Rev 2:20).

The church that tolerated her was rebuked (Rev 2:20). Even so, Christ gave her "space to repent" (Rev 2:21). The warning is real, and so is the mercy. The opposite of Jezebel is "a woman that feareth the LORD" (Pro 31:30).
roots_summary: Proper name Jezebel (1Ki 21:25) → English jezebel, a wicked, scheming woman (OED, 1558, John Knox).
roots_lines: 1Ki 21:25: Jezebel "stirred up" Ahab to wickedness
Rev 2:20: the false prophetess of Thyatira
1558: OED’s earliest evidence for the noun, John Knox
usage: "The novel cast her as the town’s Jezebel."
Whom Jezebel his wife stirred up. (1Ki 21:25).
A woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised. (Pro 31:30).

pos: noun (a traitor who betrays under the guise of friendship)
etymology: From the proper name Judas Iscariot. The American Heritage Dictionary traces the name through Late Latin and Greek to Hebrew yĕhûdâ, Judah, and defines the noun as one who betrays another under the guise of friendship. The Oxford English Dictionary’s earliest evidence for the noun is from 1396.
biblical_def: A Judas is a traitor, especially one who betrays a friend while pretending to love him. The name belongs to the disciple who sold Christ: "What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver" (Mat 26:15). He gave the sign with a kiss: "Hail, master; and kissed him" (Mat 26:49). Christ named the treachery to his face: "Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?" (Luk 22:48). David had foreseen it: "mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me" (Psa 41:9). The Christian observation: Judas walked with Christ, heard his teaching and saw his works, and still betrayed him. Nearness to holy things does not save a man. Only Christ himself does.
webster_summary: A traitor who betrays under the guise of friendship (OED, from 1396). After Judas Iscariot, who sold Christ for thirty pieces of silver and betrayed him with a kiss (Mat 26:15; Luk 22:48).
webster_full: JUDAS, n. (from 1396, OED) One who betrays another under the guise of friendship (American Heritage Dictionary). After Judas Iscariot.
See also the entry for the man himself, Judas.
scriptures: And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver.
And forthwith he came to Jesus, and said, Hail, master; and kissed him.
But Jesus said unto him, Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?
Psa 41:9
Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.
corruption_summary: "Judas" is now a name for anyone who leaves a team or a party. Scripture uses it for the man who walked with Christ and sold him, a warning that closeness to holy things is not salvation.
corruption_paragraphs: Fans call a player who changes teams a Judas, and partisans call a defector the same. That makes betrayal a matter of loyalty to a side. The original Judas betrayed the Son of God for money, with a kiss.

The warning is for insiders. Judas was one of the twelve. Christ said, "Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?" (Joh 6:70). A man can sit close to the things of God and still sell his Master. Every disciple should examine his own heart before he calls anyone else a Judas.
roots_summary: Hebrew yĕhûdâ (Judah) → Greek Ioudas → Late Latin Iūdas → English Judas, a traitor (OED, 1396).
roots_lines: Mat 26:15: thirty pieces of silver
Luk 22:48: "betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?"
1396: OED’s earliest evidence for the noun
usage: "He trusted his partner, and his partner turned Judas."
Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss? (Luk 22:48).
Mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted … hath lifted up his heel against me. (Psa 41:9).

etymology: From the proper name Jehu, king of Israel, of whom the watchman said, "he driveth furiously" (2Ki 9:20). The Oxford English Dictionary’s earliest evidence for the noun is from 1682, in the writing of John Dryden. The American Heritage Dictionary notes that Jehu is proverbially known for his swift chariot driving.
biblical_def: In English a Jehu is a fast or furious driver. The word comes from one line of Scripture. As Jehu’s chariot came on toward Jezreel, the watchman said, "the driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi; for he driveth furiously" (2Ki 9:20). Jehu was anointed to judge the house of Ahab, and he did it with the same speed and force. He boasted, "Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD" (2Ki 10:16). Yet the same chapter gives God’s verdict on the man: "But Jehu took no heed to walk in the law of the LORD God of Israel with all his heart" (2Ki 10:31). The Christian observation: Jehu drove hard at the work he was given and kept his own idols. Zeal that is loud about God’s cause and careless about God’s law is not the zeal God wants.
webster_summary: A fast or furious driver (OED, from 1682). After Jehu, who "driveth furiously" (2Ki 9:20) and boasted of zeal, yet "took no heed to walk in the law of the LORD" (2Ki 10:31).
webster_full: JEHU, n. (from 1682, OED) A fast or furious driver. After Jehu son of Nimshi, proverbial for swift chariot driving (2Ki 9:20; American Heritage Dictionary).
See also the entry for the king himself, Jehu.
scriptures: And the watchman told, saying, He came even unto them, and cometh not again: and the driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi; for he driveth furiously.
And he said, Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD. So they made him ride in his chariot.
But Jehu took no heed to walk in the law of the LORD God of Israel with all his heart: for he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam, which made Israel to sin.
corruption_summary: The word remembers only Jehu’s speed. Scripture remembers that his loud zeal for the LORD stopped short of his own heart.
corruption_paragraphs: A Jehu is a joke about a heavy foot on the pedal. The Bible’s Jehu is a warning. He did the work God gave him, and did it fast, but he invited men to admire his zeal (2Ki 10:16).
God looked further: "Jehu took no heed to walk in the law of the LORD God of Israel with all his heart" (2Ki 10:31). Energy in God’s cause does not excuse disobedience in a man’s own life.
roots_summary: Proper name Jehu (2Ki 9:20) → English jehu, a furious driver (OED, 1682, John Dryden).
roots_lines: 2Ki 9:20: "he driveth furiously"
2Ki 10:31: zeal without a whole heart
1682: OED’s earliest evidence for the noun, John Dryden
usage: "The cab driver was a regular Jehu through the downtown traffic."
For he driveth furiously. (2Ki 9:20).
But Jehu took no heed to walk in the law of the LORD. (2Ki 10:31).
